en: The *Amoghapāśa* Dharma of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—this is translated as "Fearlessness" (*amogha*) or "Vastness.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Khotan, there was a lay devotee who, with a sincere mind, maintained the recitation of the mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
He vowed to behold the Great Sage, yet after many years had passed, his long-cherished wish remained unfulfilled. Nevertheless, he held fast to his resolve.
Without slackening his redoubled diligence,
he later heard a voice in the air one night saying:
"Go to a neighboring country and visit such-and-such a king there."
Following these instructions, the practitioner went to that kingdom.
He heard that the king’s laws were extremely severe and cruel;
anyone who committed an offense was invariably punished.
The practitioner then went to see the king;
having received his patronage, he informed him of what he desired.
Consequently, he was granted his original request and entered the inner palace.
Everything was exactly like a buddha-field.
The King was none other than Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The practitioner addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"In the governance and transformation of the Great Sage, how could there be any use for execution?
Wherein lies his great compassion?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to restrain.
Out of compassion for them, I have guided them by dividing my body to become their king;
those who are executed are all merely transformed humans."
"If I can cause those fierce customs to fear my majesty and follow my influence,
such that my administrative decrees are successfully established, I shall then withdraw.
The practitioner was detained by the king for several months.
Having attained realization of the Mahāyāna, he then took his leave to return home;
[the Bodhisattva] silently granted permission.
The practitioner addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
It is my good fortune as a disciple to have encountered the Great Sage’s compassion and been granted the opportunity to see and hear the Dharma.
Having personally received his compassionate transformation for twelve years, I have now finally attained this realization.
Those who, in future ages, seek to see a bodhisattva,
yet do not change their long-held resolve and undergo diligent toil for a long time,
will achieve nothing in vain.
If a single thought of doubt arises, one will incur the offense of slandering the Dharma.
I pray that, out of compassion, you will reveal the essential teachings for the future.
The Bodhisattva replied:
I possess the mantra syllables of the Amoghapāśa;
I now bestow them upon you.
Their ritual offerings are simple and easy to perform.
Furthermore, even if the time available is not long,
if you recite and uphold this with a sincere heart,
I shall manifest my body to fulfill all your wishes.
Having received these instructions, the practitioner returned to his native land to propagate them.
Among the lay devotees in the Five Indies who attained spiritual efficacy, their number was not limited to one;
provided they practiced diligently according to the teachings, all beheld the Bodhisattva.
This is the Amoghapāśa-mantra of Avalokiteśvara, a bridge across the five turbidities and a raft for the ocean of suffering. It is said:
*Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya.*
Nikāya tadyathā amrahe pramrahe vimrahe taraha saprabiyahe iriṇi ciriṇi giriṇi aruhe niruhe dharaṇi dhāraṇi dhāpāne avatāre sarvataḥ.
raṇe raṇe paraṇe aparaṇe napha napha naphane nana nana nanane dhuna dhune dhunane samillatāntum aśmanāparabuddhane yanamo 'ryāvalokiteśvara.
*Nyasa svāhā*. Furthermore, if one who maintains the recitation of this mantra stays in a secluded and pure place or an araṇya,
and before a śarīra-stūpa, performs offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara according to their capacity and bathes with purity.
Eating pure food, dwell alone in a place of practice and maintain the recitation for one day and one night;
at dawn, the Great Sage shall appear.
All their vows are fulfilled;
they are loved and respected by all people;
and they attain the knowledge of past lives.
One will be able to realize the samādhis of the ten stages manifesting before one.
Even if one has committed the five heinous crimes,
one shall see [the deity] after two days and nights of fasting and lodging in the rain.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva King had spoken this mantra, he addressed the practitioner, saying:
"This mantra possesses great supernatural power;
it can extinguish all karmic obstructions of sentient beings."
One will swiftly obtain divine efficacy, and all that is sought will be fulfilled as desired.
If one wishes to recite this mantra to seek a vision of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
the ritual procedures for binding, protection, empowerment, and offering should be performed in accordance with the Mahātantra Susiddhikara Sūtra.
Furthermore, according to the sequence taught in the *Vajraśekhara-yoga*,
one must first recite [the mantra] with a sincere mind for one thousand times at a pure location or in an araṇya.
Whether in a mountain forest or a pure monastery, one should duly establish a maṇḍala for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara before a śarīra stūpa,
and place an image of Avalokiteśvara therein.
According to one's capacity, offer sincere worship with devotion;
bathe thoroughly in purity and don fresh, clean garments;
carefully guard the three karmas and do not forget to maintain equanimity toward joy and anger.
For one day and one night, remaining alone and ceasing all speech,
with a mind not distracted by other objects, one should single-mindedly contemplate Avalokiteśvara and recite this mantra without interruption.
Burn aloeswood incense or incense blended with the five flavors;
do not allow the smoke of the incense to be interrupted.
With mindfulness succeeding one another in an uninterrupted stream, single-mindedly seek to behold the Bodhisattva.
At each of the four corners of the mandala, place one incense burner.
Furthermore, at each corner, place one cup of fragrant water:
one consisting of honey syrup and one consisting of pure cow’s milk.
The first is saffron-scented water;
the second is ordinary white sandalwood-scented water.
As for the offerings of cakes, fruits, gruel, parched grain, and so forth:
The food offerings presented at dawn must all be collected back at the time of the daily midday meal;
they should then be placed in a clean location to be given to crows and birds.
Furthermore, fresh food and drink were prepared and offered;
by evening, these were sent away as before.
Again, fresh preparations were made and offered until daybreak, so that throughout the night and day one might not fall into sloth or indolence, fearing it would be difficult to behold [the deity].
Furthermore, one should contemplate that from within the *ūrṇā* mark on the Bodhisattva’s brow, two rays of light emerge.
One ray enters directly into all the hells,
rescuing suffering sentient beings and causing them to attain liberation.
A single ray of light comes and enters the crown of the practitioner’s head;
one should imagine it pervading their entire body,
whereby all evils and various karmic actions are completely eliminated.
With inner and outer purity,
if you contemplate, recite, and maintain a sincere mind in this way, you will surely see me.
I shall manifest my body for you and fulfill all your aspirations.
"You should receive and uphold this.
Even if there are those who have previously committed the five grave offenses of immediate retribution,
if they recite it with diligent application for two days and two nights, they will certainly behold [the deity]."
How much more so for one who is fundamentally pure?
This is the method for painting an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Fearless and Observant, excluding those who lack a sincere heart.
One is named Amoghapāśa Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
His form is like that of a Pāramitā Bodhisattva;
he has three eyes and four arms, sits upon a white lion throne, with his head turned to the left and his gaze directed downward toward his knee, wearing a jeweled crown.
Adorned before him with white lotus flowers,
he holds a phoenix-headed *vīṇā* lute with both hands,
while his left hand grasps a makara fish.
Her right hand holds a white *śrīvatsa* bird;
her left leg is bent upon the neck of a lion,
while her right leg hangs down, adorned with celestial garments and necklaces.
His entire body is ablaze with light, and his countenance is compassionate.
Observe his mudrā carefully to the left: he joins his two palms like lotus buds, with the two *vāyu* fingers (ring fingers) hooked at the heart.
At each occurrence of the word *svāhā*, [he performs this].
Immediately move the hook.
With a sincere heart, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times without distraction; this constitutes the practice for a single sitting.
One must dispatch an assistant to hold the prayer beads and keep count.
In this manner, one should perform these rituals three times each day.
This is the *āmañja* rite of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
